text: Cassini spent more than 13 years in the Saturn system, so its surfaces and instruments were exposed to possible hitchhiking microbes from Earth. If the spacecraft had simply drifted, gravity could nudge it toward one of Saturn's ocean moons, especially Enceladus or Titan. A soft or hard landing there would carry terrestrial life onto a body scientists suspect has liquid water. Crashing into Saturn's atmosphere burned the probe up, keeping it away from the moons. The final plunge also gave scientists a last chance to sample Saturn's upper atmosphere, and the disintegration of the spacecraft made a natural landing on a moon far less likely. That avoided contaminating Enceladus and the other candidate worlds.

Your stationary leg is what's doing the work. When you're not pushing, that leg has to hold the board steady and your body upright, so it goes into isometric tension. The hip, knee and ankle are all loaded at the same time. If you've got any weakness there, the leg takes on the whole imbalance. Most people don't realize that the moving leg is the one relaxed, and the still leg is the one aching.

The cause is usually your stance. If your shoulders aren't square to the board, your hips have to fight the lean, and the stationary leg takes the brunt of that. Keep your feet flat, shoulders aligned with the board, and don't let the deck tip. A lot of riders tense the whole body instead of relaxing the shoulders and arms. That tension travels down into the legs and makes the static leg hurt.

A practical fix is to stand with knees slightly bent, weight centered, and let the stationary leg do just enough to hold position. If you're pushing, that leg is doing the power, so it will naturally tire, but if it hurts even when you're just riding, check your stance first. One thing people often miss is that the push itself isn't the trigger; it's the continuous correction you're making with the stationary leg.

I'd say the pain usually eases once you stop gripping the board with your whole body. A cheap fix is to stand with your weight more over the front foot, which shifts some load away from the back leg. If your board is dragging or scraping, you're forcing extra correction. For most skaters, a few minutes of riding with a loose upper body removes the ache. If the pain keeps coming back, have a physio look at the ankle or knee, because the still leg is the one doing the balancing.

Basically it's about ancestry and cultural identity, not where someone currently lives. "Afro-American" became common after Malcolm X started using the term as a self-chosen label for people of African descent in the United States. It doesn't mean everyone was born in Africa. Most African Americans are not recent immigrants, but the name keeps a link to Africa through generations of West and Central African ancestry brought over in the slave trade. That ancestry is real, even when a family can't name a specific village. The term also covers cultural practice, for example in music and dance. So "Afro" is a marker of shared descent and culture, not a passport. It was a way for Black Americans to stop being named by outsiders and choose a term that acknowledges the African root and American life. A lot of people are confused because the label sounds like it describes current residence. It doesn't. The prefix points to the diaspora connection. Even families with mixed ancestry often recognize some African heritage. That recognition is the point. The term carries political weight, as a way to assert a connection to the continent and its peoples rather than only a racial category.

The main routes are cross-border from Iraq and Lebanon, with black-market brokers running smuggling channels. Iraqi and Lebanese gunrunners move stock through informal networks, often paid per crate. The war has gone on for years now, so resupply is a constant need. Local production can't keep up, and even when borders get tight, weapons still move because armed groups on every side need them to stay in the fight. Once a supply line opens, it keeps running while the fighting goes on. It's a matter of keeping the conflict fed.

Basically it's not that all drugs are bad. The problem isn't pleasure; it's how pleasure gets regulated in the brain. Heroine and cocaine hit the same reward pathway, but the brain responds by dialing that pathway down. Repeated dosing means you need more for the same high, the baseline low gets worse, and quitting produces real withdrawal symptoms. That's the core reason people call drugs bad, and it's the part the question doesn't see. A drug that only gave a fixed high without changing the system could exist in principle, but the body doesn't tolerate a new chemical without adapting to it.

The second issue is dose. Most drugs have a steep dose-response curve. A small amount does little, a normal amount produces the effect you want, and a larger amount quickly tips into toxicity. Alcohol is a good common example. A couple of drinks is fine for most people, but the gap between a pleasant buzz and a dangerous or lethal dose is narrower than people expect. You can measure blood alcohol concentration at the bar, but the curve still rises fast enough that judgment goes before coordination.

People often ask about drugs with zero adverse effects, and the practical answer is that zero means the effect and the damage share the same molecule. Nicotine is a useful example because it's not as violently pleasurable as heroin or cocaine, yet it's still classified as addictive because of how the brain adapts to it. If a substance were truly zero-effect beyond the intended one, it would have to leave the nervous system exactly as it found it every time, which is rare.

The third reason is how we actually take drugs. A perfect molecule can still be ruined by how it's administered. Snorting cocaine or injecting heroin adds infection risk, and smoking anything adds lung burden. A drug with a wide therapeutic window would help, but people use drugs in settings where that window is tested daily, so the real-world outcome is worse than the chemistry alone would predict.

That's why we call them bad, not because pleasure is bad, but because the pleasure comes with adaptation, dose limits, and withdrawal, and those things don't cancel out just because the high feels good.

Hi,

Yeah, that pain is real, and it is usually a cumulative overload response. Following your wife through shops exposes you to crowds, bright lights, noise, and a lot of decisions. Your jaw, temples, neck and shoulders tighten, and stress hormones and dehydration make it worse. A normal headache is usually one trigger, while this builds up slowly across the day. It is not you being fussy. Give your eyes some rest, drink water, take short breaks, and try not to keep pushing through a full day. If it gets sharp or comes with nausea, it's worth checking with a doctor.

Alex

Hi,

What your brother was doing sounds like a little attention or word-response check. He wasn't testing whether you could speak; he was seeing how you react when you have to repeat and spell a word, then answer a plain question.

Your "milk" answer is easy to explain. Cows and milk are a very strong pair in our heads. After you'd been saying and spelling silk, your mind was on words and associations, so when he asked what cows drink, the milk link came out before your conscious thought caught up. It was an automatic response, not that you actually think cows drink milk. You weren't confused about the fact; the question just triggered the obvious association first.

If it happens again, you can just say water. He probably wanted to see how you answer under a bit of pressure. He might have been checking whether you can tell what's real from what just pops into your head.

Hope that makes sense.

Sam

Hi,
The first thing is to get pre-qualified for a loan, because it changes what you can actually buy. Don't estimate your own budget. Ask the bank what they'll lend and write that number down.
Mortgage rates and terms can move around, so lock only when you're ready to commit. A rate lock usually lasts 30 to 120 days, and your lender can tell you the price for an extension if you fall behind.
The house inspection is the part people underestimate. You're paying a third party to find problems you'd otherwise miss, and the report can become a negotiation tool. If serious defects come up, ask the seller for repairs or a price reduction. Don't waive the inspection; that's how buyers end up paying for someone else's mistake.
Closing costs are another real cost on top of the price, like lender fees, title insurance, transfer taxes and registration. Ask the lender for an estimate before you sign anything.
Keep your documents in one folder, and send them to the lender early. If you're buying with a partner or family member, get the ownership arrangement and responsibility for mortgage payments written down.
Talk to me when you have the numbers.
Alex

Hi Mark,

You can actually tell the difference just by looking at the label. The big chemical distinction is the type of surfactant. A standard shampoo and a 2-in-1 conditioner both rely on anionic surfactants. A 3-in-1, however, almost always uses amphoteric surfactants. That makes it milder. The amphoteric chemistry doesn't lather quite as much and isn't as aggressive, so it is gentler on hair and skin. Anionic surfactants are better at cutting grease, while amphoteric ones balance cleaning with conditioning.

The tradeoff is real. A regular shampoo cleans deeper but strips the hair of its natural oils. A 3-in-1 does a weaker job of washing away buildup. It also has the conditioning effect, which means your hair stays softer, but you might need to use it less often to avoid it feeling sticky. For a 3-in-1 to work on both skin and hair, it can't be harsh enough to do a deep clean. It sacrifices cleaning power to be safe for daily use on sensitive skin.

I use it for quick washes when I have nothing else, but for my hair, I prefer a dedicated shampoo for a real clean. The 3-in-1 is a convenience product for people who skip the separate steps when they have the time. If you wash your hair every day, a dedicated shampoo and conditioner is better for hair health.

Let me know if you want a specific product recommendation.

Sam

Hi,

They use GPS, and satellite laser ranging. The main tool is a network of GPS receivers bolted to bedrock on each plate. A receiver locks onto a constellation of GPS satellites and works out its position to a few millimeters. The receivers are surveyed repeatedly over weeks to years, and the difference in position, divided by the elapsed time, gives the plate's velocity. A single plate has one coherent velocity field, so any two stations on the same plate give consistent results.

The rates are slow, a few centimeters a year. The Pacific Plate drifts about 7 to 8 cm per year, the North American Plate around 2 cm. GPS can catch that motion in a year, which is why you can actually track a whole continent's path on a map.

One caveat is that GPS only works on land, so ocean floor motion comes from satellite laser ranging to satellites, which also works in millimeters.

Mark

Inbreeding makes relatives share ancestors, so the same copies of harmful recessive genes become more likely to meet in an offspring. Most people carry several recessive variants that affect development and the nervous system. In a non-inbred mating, harmful recessive variants are often hidden behind a normal copy. With closer kinship, the chance that both parents pass the same variant rises, so harmful combinations are exposed more often.

For IQ, the relationship is probabilistic, not automatic. More inbreeding raises the risk of genetic defects and developmental problems that can lower measured IQ, but some inbred offspring have average scores. It does not mean every child of relatives is less intelligent; it changes probabilities. Scientists usually use the inbreeding coefficient to estimate this risk. The central idea is inbreeding depression. Higher homozygosity increases the chance that harmful recessive alleles are expressed, and this can affect the brain and cognition.

An injury to the arm often seems less painful than the same injury elsewhere for the same force because the arm has more soft-tissue padding. The upper arm and forearm contain a thick layer of muscle and fat under relatively thick skin. Those tissues absorb and spread out impact, and they shift during movement, which reduces pressure on deeper structures.

The arm still has many sensory nerves, and a cut or bruise can be very painful. The face has dense nerve supply, and the legs carry body weight. The arm’s muscle bulk and its mobility make it feel less painful than an injury to the face or torso. The torso also guards vital organs, which makes a hit there more alarming. Actual pain still depends on how deep the injury is and how much swelling develops. A broken bone or joint injury hurts far more than a shallow cut.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells much more strongly than oxygen does. Hemoglobin is the protein that normally carries oxygen from the lungs to your organs. CO has roughly 200 to 250 times the binding strength of oxygen, so even small inhaled amounts can occupy most hemoglobin sites. The resulting carboxyhemoglobin cannot deliver oxygen, so tissues starve. CO also shifts oxygen release from hemoglobin, so even the oxygen already bound is less available to tissues. That effect makes even a moderate CO level harder to recover from. CO exposure therefore causes headache, dizziness, confusion, and loss of consciousness before you notice an alarm.

Carbon dioxide, by contrast, is a normal waste gas that healthy lungs remove efficiently. At typical indoor levels it does not compete well with oxygen for hemoglobin, and the body regulates its level through breathing rate. High CO2 can make you drowsy and can be harmful. The ordinary exposure that makes CO dangerous is not CO2. A typical safe indoor CO2 level is below 1000 ppm, and many offices aim for around 400 to 600 ppm. Above that, people get tired. Carbon monoxide becomes dangerous far below such thresholds, often around 50 to 100 ppm sustained for minutes to hours, depending on exposure time. CO is also colorless, odorless, and hard to detect, which is why people may inhale it in rooms with poor ventilation or running engines. In a house, furnace problems and appliance leaks are common sources. A CO detector should be placed near sleeping areas and on each floor. Carbon monoxide alarms are not carbon dioxide alarms. Indoor CO2 monitors and CO monitors serve different jobs, so do not treat them as interchangeable. Keep appliance vents clear and test CO detectors monthly in each room.

The brace position protects passengers by holding the head, torso, and limbs together during a sudden stop or crash landing. In an emergency, you cross your arms over your chest, let one hand hold the other elbow, bend your head down, and keep your feet flat on the floor. This keeps your head and limbs from flying forward when the plane suddenly slows down. If you do not brace, your body keeps moving even after the plane stops, so your head, chest, and hands can hit seats, floors, or other passengers. The crossed-arm position reduces the chance of a whiplash or broken arm. It also stops you from slamming into the seat in front or the cabin walls.

Passengers should listen for the brace call, drop their heads, and stay still until told to move. Crew and passengers get practice because the call can come suddenly during takeoff, landing, or turbulence. Bracing does not make a crash survivable by magic. It limits how far your body moves inside the cabin. The position works best when everyone does it at the same time, so the cabin interior stops being the thing that hurts you.

Why aren't there any well known businesses that existed before the industrial era? Most early businesses were small local trades. Their names never left the town. The few large ones, like chartered trading companies, were famous among merchants but not to the general public. Broad familiarity needs scale plus infrastructure such as railways, telegraphs, printing, and later broadcast media. These spread names widely. The Industrial Revolution and 20th-century mass production and advertising turned firms into brands that households recognize. Old records were often lost and many names changed when firms merged or were absorbed. Their fame was local or confined to specialists.

The dealer quote can be low while the car itself costs more. I have bought cars both ways, and the pattern is consistent. You get a rate lower than the bank, but the dealer also marks up the invoice by adding prep fees, protection packages, or a higher vehicle price. The math ends up the same as a higher bank rate: more total interest.

My first car was financed at a dealer with a very attractive advertised rate. The sticker price was higher than the same model at two other dealerships, and the salesperson bundled in an extended warranty and a paint sealant package that I did not need. When I asked for the loan amount, it was $3200 more than the car's actual market value. The lower rate did not save me anything; I paid extra on top.

Banks price the loan directly. You walk in with a car you have already priced from several dealers. The bank gives you a stated rate and a stated amount. You see the total cost before signing. With a dealer, the rate is often only part of the deal. The car price and fees can move independently of the interest rate.

I have seen a dealer offer a 4% rate when the bank offered 5.5%, yet the dealer's loan was $8000 while the bank's was $7100. The extra car cost wiped out the rate advantage. The dealer's lower rate is the bait; the higher vehicle price is the hook.

There is another angle: banks usually have no dealer add-ons to negotiate. You can compare three banks on rate, term and fee. A dealer controls both sides of the transaction, which gives them room to shift money around. If the car is worth $20,000 but the dealer invoices it at $21,500, you are financing $1,500 that is not really part of the car.

My rule now is simple. I find the car price from at least three places, then go to the bank with that number. If the dealer wants to beat the bank's total cost, they have to show it in the final payment and total interest, not just the headline rate.

The lower dealer rate is real, but it is not the whole bill. The bank wins on total cost because it does not get to inflate the car price. The dealer wins on perception, and often you end up paying more overall.

I'm on the side of letting states decide, but the patchwork is turning into its own kind of mess. Colorado legalizes it and Oregon does too, while neighboring Kansas still treats a joint like a hard crime. Drive across a line with a joint in your pocket and the answer to "is it legal here?" depends on which side of the road you're on. What annoys me is the mismatch between state law and federal law. Congress still calls marijuana a Schedule I drug, so your state's green light doesn't shield you from a federal prosecution. A doctor can prescribe it in some states, and a pharmacy in Texas can sell it in another, and nobody has fixed the gap. The patchwork gives states their freedom, but until Washington D.C. agrees with the states, this whole thing stays half-baked.

I've always assumed the body ran on electricity like a tiny battery, but the real source is ions crossing cell membranes. Every cell maintains a voltage by using ATP-driven pumps that push three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, keeping the interior negative. When a nerve fires, sodium channels snap open and the sudden inflow of sodium flips the membrane potential; then potassium rushes out to bring it back down. That brief wave is what moves a thought or a muscle twitch. The body doesn't store electric charge magically; it stores chemical energy as ion gradients, then releases it as a current. It is chemistry, not sparks.

Sampling older songs is not a shortcut. It is a way to make old recordings work inside a new track, but it demands both an ear and a lawyer. Most people think of sampling as copying, and sometimes they are right, but the interesting work happens when a producer cuts a short passage and rebuilds it until it behaves differently. You take a few seconds of a record, chop it into smaller pieces, slow it down, pitch it, loop it, and layer it under something new. The goal is not to hide the source, but to let the original melody, voice or groove carry the mood of the new song.

In practice, a producer usually starts with a groove or a vocal phrase that works hard. They might find a drum break, a bass line, or a horn hit that can stand on its own. That fragment is then processed until it fits the tempo and tonal center of the new track. A sample can be stretched, reversed, sliced, filtered or run through a synthesizer, so the same four-second piece can become something that sounds entirely different. Sometimes the whole track hangs on a two-bar loop, and the producer has to decide how much of the old record to keep before the original song starts to fight the new arrangement. Finding usable material takes patience. A good loop has clear transients and clean separation, and a producer may spend hours auditioning records before choosing one. The legal side is just as important as the sonic side. Because a recording involves both the composer’s copyright and the label’s master rights, clearing a sample usually means negotiating with both the writers and the record company. If the master cannot be cleared, a producer may re-record the melody with new instruments, which is a different legal path but still needs the writers’ permission. Clearance deals are often written contracts, and the fees can become a significant cost.

The classic example is “Rapper’s Delight” from 1979. It used the opening of “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” by The Exciters and turned a short soul passage into the backbone of a hit. That record did not replace the older song. It gave the older song a second life and introduced hip-hop to a much wider audience. It showed how a sample can honor a previous artist while making space for something new.

The trick is restraint. Producers often fail when they layer too many sources or let the original recording fight the new arrangement. A good sample stays recognizably itself but serves the new composition. When it works, the listener hears the old song and the new song at the same time. That double hearing makes sampling a musical practice rather than a borrowing exercise.

I stand by the idea that a headache is a signal from my nervous system. For me, the pain starts as a dull band around my temples and climbs toward the back of my neck. The trigger is rarely one thing. A missed meal, poor sleep, or a stiff neck can set off irritation in the trigeminal nerve and blood-vessel changes that make the area feel tight and sensitive. I have learned to notice small signs before they turn into a full migraine. A flicker in one eye, a metallic taste, or pressure behind one eye tells me I need to rest. When I catch the attack early and sit in a dark room, the pain often eases. If it becomes sharp, pulsing, or comes with nausea, I treat it as a migraine and take the medicine my doctor gave me. The details matter more than the word stress.

I can’t even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We picked this place specifically because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel, and we arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday thinking it'd be easy. We put our names into their useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and there was no line at all. Our bill came out to around $130, which felt pretty steep to me. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn't offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were a bit interesting. The problem was there simply were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any.

Overall, I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. If the line is long, I'd probably think it over.

Keeping it, four out of five stars. The space bar rattles, and hitting it with the edge of my thumb sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats then and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking. I paid $38 and kept it anyway because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison. My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap space bar a little closer to the middle.

I’ve lived around Vegas most of my life, mostly the under-21 side, so I’ve already seen a lot of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn was one I finally got to see. My impression was mixed, maybe a bit worse than mixed.

The good part first: that circular stage actually works. You look down into it, and from nearly any seat you get a decent view. That’s unusual for Vegas. A few acts were genuinely strong, especially the strength stuff, the aerialists, and the divers. They’re clearly athletes. But a lot of it felt familiar, like Cirque du Soleil. Not a copy, just a similar level of feat. If you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable things done with more clarity.

Clarity was the weak spot. What’s the story? Still not sure. There’s a dream, maybe. A man. Water. It came across as pretty images without the show explaining what it meant. Too much was going on at once, too many people and elements and stacked wow moments. A more restrained show would probably hit harder. It fell into the usual Vegas idea that more has to be better, so they packed everything in.

One practical note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, there’s a discount. It’s $99 rather than the usual $125. That helps. I probably won’t see it again and wouldn’t pay for a second showing. Apart from a handful of stunts, it was average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was. That said, a few friends enjoyed it, and if you haven’t seen it, maybe go once. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The sales rep wrote the address down wrong. Her handwritten “7” looked like a “1,” so the shirts for 5407 went to 5401 instead. The people at 5401 took the box to the local UPS store to send it back to the sender. It just vanished, and we didn’t find out about it until several weeks later. While the dispute was going on, we put in another order for two shirts. Rockmount wouldn’t refund the first two. The owner was the one dealing with it. He admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address, but said we’d have to get the shirts back before getting money. He also said our part was being too cold to the neighbors at 5401, only four doors down. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and in the end it gave us the credit.
